scenario.title: Stage a recovery file without replacing the current configuration
scenario.summary: Retrieve the published file from a TFTP server, inspect its bytes and protect existing device files.
scenario.objective:
Download Recovery/public/recovery.cfg to Device/staged.cfg using the supplied TFTP service.

Keep Device/current.cfg, Device/note.txt and the published recovery file unchanged.

Keep the TFTP transfer path ready across all supplied files and transfer ports. A staged file is not an activated configuration.
scenario.retry_guidance: Read the failed stage or case, inspect the named source and destination files, and retry. A transfer report and completion are different results.

guide.title: Understand the file roles
guide.why: A server supplies files; a client requests an operation. Here Device is the client. You have already explored IP endpoints and UDP in the transport unit; no terminal command or equipment setup is needed.
guide.action: Read the concepts and different worked example before opening the workspace.

guide.title: Try the separate training handover
guide.why: Use the provided training files to observe actual transfers and specific failures.
guide.action: Keep the starter’s public/retired.cfg and select Transfer file. Open Actual transfer, inspect lesson.cfg, then select Check example.

guide.title: Complete the independent assignment
guide.why: Complete every file, preservation and current-path requirement independently.
guide.action: Use the supplied file-transfer controls and policy editor where present. Transfer files, inspect actual results, then Check work.

scenario.explanation: The request must retrieve the published recovery bytes and write a separate staged name. TFTP begins at UDP69, then uses the supplied transfer ports for DATA and ACK. Every sample has its own source bytes, so copying a look-alike retired file cannot satisfy the complete task. Staging does not activate the file or change the current configuration.
hints: Read the supplied goal and server file list. The retired file is a real, transferable file, but not the requested replacement.
Download reads Recovery and writes Device. Use the new staged name; preserve current.cfg.
Inspect the actual DATA source port and ACK destination port. UDP port 69 is only the initial request endpoint.
scenario.simplifications: Primary sources checked2026-11-13: current CCNA v1.1 objective4.9, RFC1350 and RFC959. Only supplied virtual endpoints/files; byte-preserving UTF8 fixtures, TFTP octet requests/DATA/ACK with fixed representative transfer ports, FTP passive TCP opening and named training-login admission. No real client, host files, packets, authentication exchange, encryption, protocol codec, ASCII/netascii conversion, active FTP, retransmission, timer, closing or full equipment behavior. Failed transfers leave the destination unchanged in this atomic exercise; real interruptions can leave partial files.

presentation.goal: Retrieve a server file into a new device name and verify the actual result.
requirements: Download Recovery/public/recovery.cfg to Device/staged.cfg using the supplied TFTP service.
Keep Device/current.cfg, Device/note.txt and the published recovery file unchanged.
Keep the TFTP transfer path ready across all supplied files and transfer ports. A staged file is not an activated configuration.
presentation.context: A server supplies files; a client requests an operation. Here Device is the client. You have already explored IP endpoints and UDP in the transport unit; no terminal command or equipment setup is needed.

concepts.title: Read the direction from the device’s point of view
concepts.text: Download brings a server file onto the device. Upload sends a device file to the server. The two file fields always name Device and Server stores; changing direction changes which one is read and which one is written.

concepts.title: TFTP uses a request, data blocks and replies
concepts.text: The client sends its first request to UDP port 69. Data and acknowledgements then use the client and server transfer ports shown in Sample inputs. Each data block must be acknowledged; UDP alone does not guarantee delivery. This exercise uses byte-preserving octet mode. TFTP has no directory-listing command; use the file inventory supplied by this task.

concepts.title: A copy is not the same as a correct handover
concepts.text: Copy into a new file name so you retain the current configuration. Then inspect the new file and check the task: a successful transfer can still copy an outdated file. TFTP has no login and no encryption in this exercise; these are nonsecret training files.

worked.label: Direction
worked.explanation: Read a file supplied by the server; do not upload a device file.

worked.label: Server file
worked.explanation: This is the published training replacement, not public/retired.cfg.

worked.label: Device file
worked.explanation: A separate staged name leaves current.cfg intact.

worked.label: First packet / later traffic
worked.explanation: Only the initial request targets port 69; read the actual DATA and ACK rows after transferring.

practice.title: Inspect the first copy
practice.action: Keep the starter’s public/retired.cfg and select Transfer file. Read Actual transfer, open Inspect files, inspect lesson.cfg, then select Check example.
practice.observe: The copy succeeds, but the file requirement fails because those are retired bytes. Transfer success is not assignment completion.

practice.title: Choose the published file
practice.action: Use Fill worked transfer to populate the demonstrated request without executing it. Select Transfer file, inspect lesson.cfg and select Check example.
practice.observe: The published bytes now match in every sample; current.cfg and the operator note remain intact.

practice.title: Try the opposite direction
practice.action: Select Upload and transfer the same request. Read the file-access feedback, then return to Download and retry.
practice.observe: Upload tries to write the server’s files. This read-only recovery service cannot accept it; a failed request does not overwrite files.

review.introduction: Reviewed client/server direction, TFTP request69 versus later DATA/ACK ports, read-only/no-encryption scope and the different Gallery/Training worked copy. Actual R3 Introduction and worked table inspected; no independent novice acceptance.
review.example: Reviewed actual Transfer file, Check example, inert Fill worked transfer and Inspect files controls. Retired bytes copy successfully but fail the task; the demonstrated correction passes and the Upload exploration is refused without writing. Separate assignment state remains unchanged in widgets and native R3.
review.assignment: Reviewed the full recovery-copy checklist, Device/Server file labels, live read/write diagram and supplied port table. Three source-held file/endpoint cases grade exact staged bytes and preserved originals. Wrong-source copy clears success; selected reset/resume and Challenge guidance are tested. Actual R3 Assignment inspected.

A write-capable training login and correct upload direction copy the original local file into the archive. Compare all sample ports. The outward rule targets the passive service range; the return rule uses that range as its source and the device’s client port as its destination.
A copy of the right bytes, current transfer readiness and the denied Telnet flow must all pass. Keep the restrictive final rules.

presentation.goal: Make an FTP archive copy work while preserving the original files and a blocked service.
requirements: Upload Device/current.cfg to Archive/archive/branch.cfg through FTP using a supplied write-capable training login.
Repair only R1’s supplied router policy so control and every listed passive data endpoint work in both directions.
Preserve Device/current.cfg, Device/note.txt and Archive/archive/audit.cfg. Keep Telnet traffic to Archive blocked.
Verify exact archived bytes and the current transfer path across all supplied inputs.
presentation.context: The transport unit taught TCP openings, source/service ports and the native ACL document. This task adds a file operation on top. Training logins are provided choices, not real accounts or credentials.

concepts.title: Control and file data use different connections
concepts.text: FTP first opens a TCP control connection to server port 21. A successful control connection or login does not prove that file data can move. In passive mode the server supplies another listening port; the client opens that separate TCP data connection.

concepts.title: Connection direction and file direction are different
concepts.text: For this upload, Device opens both connections and sends the file. For a download, the client still opens a passive data connection, but the server sends the file bytes back. Read both source and destination ports when repairing the return policy.

concepts.title: A login can have limited permission
concepts.text: reader can inspect archive files but cannot publish a new one. archivist and backup-operator can write files under archive/. This models named-profile admission and file permission, not a real authentication exchange. Plain FTP does not encrypt these training transfers.

concepts.title: Repair the useful path without removing protection
concepts.text: Use Sample inputs to find all passive endpoints, not only the first one. Add the necessary narrow rules before the deny. Keep Telnet blocked and retain the supplied files; permitting everything is not a successful handover.

worked.label: Operation
worked.explanation: Upload preserves the local source and creates the server archive.

worked.label: Control connection
worked.value: Client 49152 → server TCP 21, with its reverse reply
worked.explanation: This already works in the practice starter.

worked.label: Passive data endpoints
worked.value: Server TCP 53010–53012; replies return to client 49152
worked.explanation: The additional connection needs rules in both directions.

worked.label: Training login
worked.explanation: Both supplied profiles can write archive/; reader cannot.

practice.title: Reproduce the data failure
practice.action: Select Transfer file without changing the starter. Open Packet and file stages under Actual transfer, then read the control, login and data-connection stages.
practice.observe: Control and login pass, but the passive data opening is filtered. No archive file is created.

practice.title: Apply the worked repair
practice.action: Select Fill worked transfer, inspect the router rules it populates, then select Transfer file and Check example.
practice.observe: The rules allow the listed passive range in both directions while keeping the final deny. The archive contains the original current.cfg bytes.

practice.title: Separate permission from connectivity
practice.action: Change Training login to reader and transfer again. Read the feedback, then choose another supplied write-capable login and retry.
practice.observe: A working connection does not grant write access. The failed request leaves the archive untouched; either supported writer can complete the task.

review.introduction: Reviewed FTP control/login versus passive data opening, client initiation versus file direction, supplied writer/reader access and retained Telnet protection. Separate PracticeVault example is taught before independent repair; actual R3 Introduction inspected.
review.example: Reviewed the actual router editor and service/direction/server/login/file controls. Starter control passes while data fails; Fill worked transfer is inert, the repair transfers real simulated bytes, reader fails and the alternate writer succeeds. Actual R3 stages, feedback, case results and practice inspected; no assignment credit awarded.
review.assignment: Reviewed independent R1 policy and archive/preservation requirements across three supplied data endpoints and different bytes. Actual R3 split workspace, narrow stacked editors, light150/dark200, wrong-source grading, retry, save and selected reset inspected. Labels and feedback distinguish a copied file from a completed task.

scenario.summary: Combine two different transfer roles, retain the original configuration and verify every sample without removing access restrictions.
scenario.objective:
Upload Device/current.cfg to Archive/archive/original.cfg using FTP and a supplied write-capable training login.

Download Recovery/public/recovery.cfg to Device/staged.cfg using TFTP. The staged replacement must not be archived as the original.

Preserve Device/current.cfg, Device/note.txt, Archive/archive/audit.cfg and Recovery/public/recovery.cfg.

Repair only R1’s router policy. Keep both transfer paths ready for every listed endpoint and retain the Telnet restriction to Archive.

scenario.explanation: The correct handover retains current.cfg, archives its original bytes through FTP, and separately retrieves the replacement through TFTP into staged.cfg. Both services need their own paths: passive FTP separates control and data, while TFTP moves from its initial request port to transfer ports. Either copy order can work. Fresh per-case source bytes and current-policy checks expose wrong-source, single-endpoint and permit-all shortcuts.
hints: Write down each copy as source → destination. The archive’s source is current.cfg; the staging source is Recovery’s published file.
FTP needs control and passive data in both directions; TFTP uses port69 only initially. Compare all supplied ports before editing policy.
A broad permit-all repair loses the required Telnet protection. Check file bytes, preserved files and readiness together.

presentation.goal: Archive the original file and stage its replacement without confusing their contents.
requirements: Upload Device/current.cfg to Archive/archive/original.cfg using FTP and a supplied write-capable training login.
Download Recovery/public/recovery.cfg to Device/staged.cfg using TFTP. The staged replacement must not be archived as the original.
Preserve Device/current.cfg, Device/note.txt, Archive/archive/audit.cfg and Recovery/public/recovery.cfg.
Repair only R1’s router policy. Keep both transfer paths ready for every listed endpoint and retain the Telnet restriction to Archive.
presentation.context: Complete the recovery-copy and passive-FTP lessons first if these roles are new. Both assignments remain visible here: the archive needs the original bytes, while the staged file needs the replacement bytes.

concepts.title: Keep original and replacement roles separate
concepts.text: An archive preserves what is stored now. A staged replacement is a different file waiting for a later decision. Copying the staged file into an archive named original does not make it the original; check actual contents rather than labels.

concepts.title: Choose the service for each server
concepts.text: Archive offers FTP with supplied write-capable login profiles and a separate passive data endpoint. Recovery offers read-only TFTP with no login. Use the service shown for that server and read upload/download from the device’s point of view.

concepts.title: A handover includes preserved work and a ready path
concepts.text: Two copied files are only part of the task. Keep current.cfg and the audit file unchanged, support every supplied transfer endpoint and retain the denied service. A repair that works for only the first sample is incomplete.

concepts.title: Verify before activating anything
concepts.text: Inspect the two destinations and compare them with their intended sources. This lab stages and archives files only; it does not activate configurations. FTP and TFTP in this exercise are unencrypted and use nonsecret training data.

worked.label: Archive original
worked.explanation: Use the original local file as the archive source.

worked.label: Stage replacement
worked.explanation: Use a new local file name; leave current.cfg intact.

worked.label: Connection paths
worked.value: FTP control 21 + passive 53010–53012; TFTP request 69 + transfer 53020–53022
worked.explanation: Use the supplied client port 49152 and retain the matching reverse paths.

worked.label: Verify independently
worked.value: Original archive and replacement stage are different byte strings
worked.explanation: The order can vary because neither operation changes current.cfg.

practice.title: Archive the original training file
practice.action: Keep FTP upload selected. Select Transfer file and inspect the failed data opening. Select Fill worked transfer to populate the worked policy/request, then Transfer file.
practice.observe: Only the original local file is archived. The staged-file requirement is still unfinished; a partial handover is not completion.

practice.title: Stage the replacement
practice.action: Select TFTP and Gallery, then Fill worked transfer and Transfer file. Inspect lesson.cfg and the archive, then Check example.
practice.observe: The staged bytes come from Gallery, while the archive still contains the original current.cfg. Both sample paths and protections pass.

practice.title: Diagnose a wrong source
practice.action: Select FTP, Upload and PracticeVault. Choose Training login archivist or backup-operator. Change Device file to lesson.cfg and Server file to archive/demo.cfg, then Transfer file and Check example. Restore current.cfg as the upload source and retry.
practice.observe: The upload itself succeeds, but the archive requirement explains that the replacement is not the original. A later correct transfer repairs the result without a reset.

review.introduction: Reviewed original-versus-staged file roles, FTP/TFTP server selection, bidirectional endpoint protection and staging without activation. Worked example uses different device/server/files/ports. Actual R3 Introduction inspected; prior two transfer lessons are explicit prerequisites.
review.example: Reviewed the actual two-transfer guided sequence and optional wrong-source exploration, including the explicit writer-login action after changing protocol. Original archive and replacement staging remain separate files; partial work and wrong bytes fail. Actual R3 practice and packet evidence inspected, with assignment isolation checked.
review.assignment: Reviewed both independent copy requirements, source/file preservation and retained blocked Telnet across three worlds. Either copy order and either supplied writer are valid in focused tests. Actual R3 Assignment, failed copies, repairs, completion, scaling and native reset inspected; no novice/platform acceptance inferred.
